chapters.title: Foundations
chapters.intro: The ground every cook stands on before a sauce is made: mise en place, the knife, heat, the stocks and the ways a liquid is thickened, cleared and seasoned. At Brennan's every sauce on the menu, from the marchand de vin to the turtle soup, starts from one of these foundations, so a cook who has them can learn any plate quickly.

entries.title: Mise en place
covers: Everything in its place: the prepared ingredients, tools and plan a cook sets before service begins
Building a station: board anchored on a damp cloth, knives, side towels, ninth pans of cut vegetables, salt, pepper and oils within reach
The prep list and the par: how much to make for the covers booked, and why a sauce cook reads the book before setting up
Mise for a sauce station: clarified butter warm, reductions made, shallots ciselé, herbs picked, stocks hot
Working clean as you go: wiping the board, clearing scraps, labelling and dating every container
Mise as a habit of mind: the cook who thinks one step ahead of the ticket
leaves: the French words for vessels, tools and bundles belong to mise-en-place-words
the knife cuts belong to knife-cuts
what each station cooks belongs to the-stations

entries.title: Knife cuts
covers: The grip and the claw: a pinch grip on the blade, fingertips curled, the knuckle as a guide

The classical sizes: brunoise about 3 mm, small dice about 6 mm, medium dice about 12 mm, large dice about 20 mm; julienne about 3 mm square and 5 to 6 cm long; bâtonnet about 6 mm square (authors confirm against the folio)
Ciseler for shallots, émincer for thin slices, chiffonade for leaves, concassée for peeled, seeded and chopped tomato
Cutting the trinity: onion, celery and green pepper in an even small dice so they soften together
Why even cuts matter: even cooking, a clean look in a clear sauce, a predictable yield
Tourner and paysanne as the cuts of the classical garnishes
Knife care at the station: honing, a keen edge, a board that never slides
leaves: the French names as words on a menu or ticket belong to cuts-by-name
the trinity itself belongs to the-holy-trinity

entries.title: Heat and the pan
covers: How heat reaches food: conduction through the pan, convection in oil, water and the oven's air, radiation from the salamander and the coals
Browning and its two reactions: the Maillard reaction of proteins and sugars, and caramelisation of sugar alone at higher heat (authors confirm the temperatures)
Water holds food at or below 100°C (212°F): why a poached or boiled food never browns, and a wet or crowded pan steams instead of searing
The heat ladder on the stove in outline: low, medium and high and what each is for, and a simmer told from a boil
Pans and what they do: heavy pans hold and spread heat, thin ones react fast; cast iron, steel, copper and non-stick each have a job, and bare aluminium reacts with acid
Carryover heat: food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, so it comes off a little early and rests
Reading heat with the senses and the probe: the sizzle, the shimmer of oil, the smell, the thermometer
leaves: sweat, sauté and sear belong to saute
poaching and the simmer belong to poaching
resting a roast belongs to roast-and-baste
temperatures for food safety belong to cooking-temperatures

entries.title: White stock
covers: Fond blanc: bones blanched or rinsed, never roasted, so the stock stays pale and clean
Chicken or veal bones in cold water, a white mirepoix of onion, celery and leek, a bouquet garni and peppercorns
Start cold, bring slowly to a bare simmer, skim the scum, never boil: boiling clouds it with fat and protein
Times: chicken about 3 to 5 hours, veal 6 to 8; strain through a chinois, cool fast, lift the fat once set
What it builds: velouté, suprême, allemande, white soups, the poaching liquor for poultry
Gelatine as the mark of a good stock: it sets to a wobble when cold
leaves: cooling it safely belongs to cooling-stocks-and-sauces
reducing it to a glace belongs to glaces

entries.title: Brown stock
covers: Fond brun: veal or beef bones roasted deep brown, never black, with a mirepoix of onion, carrot and celery
Tomato purée (the concentrate) cooked on the bones until rust coloured, the pincé, for colour and sweetness
Deglazing the roasting tray so the browned juices go into the pot, not the sink
Cold water, a bare simmer for 8 to 12 hours, steady skimming, no salt
What it builds: espagnole, demi-glace, glace de viande, jus, the marchand de vin and the whole brown family
The faults: burnt bones make it bitter, boiling makes it cloudy and greasy, salt makes it useless for reduction
leaves: glace and demi-glace belong to glaces and demi-glace

entries.title: Fumet de poisson
covers: Fish stock made fast: bones and heads of lean white fish, gills removed, rinsed of blood
Sweat the bones with onion, celery or fennel and mushroom trim in butter, add white wine, then cold water
Twenty to thirty minutes only: longer draws out bitterness from the bones
Lean fish frames such as sole, flounder, snapper or redfish; oily fish such as salmon make it strong and greasy
Shellfish stock as the Louisiana cousin: shrimp heads and shells, crab bodies, the base of a seafood gumbo
What it builds: fish velouté, sauce vin blanc, normande, Bercy, the poaching liquor for fish
leaves: court-bouillon and nage belong to court-bouillon-and-nage
the seafood gumbo build belongs to seafood-gumbo
fish velouté and its daughters belong to veloute-family

entries.title: Court-bouillon and nage
covers: Court-bouillon, the short broth: water, an acid (wine, vinegar or lemon), aromatics and salt, simmered 20 to 30 minutes before the food goes in
Its job is to flavour and to poach: whole fish, shellfish, sweetbreads; the acid firms flesh and keeps it white
Cooking in it: fish laid in at a bare simmer, never boiled; a whole fish started cold, portions started hot
Nage: a court-bouillon made fine enough to serve, often reduced and mounted with butter, as in à la nage
The Louisiana seafood boil as a court-bouillon taken to the limit of salt, cayenne and lemon
Why the French court-bouillon is not the Creole courtbouillon, a thick tomato and roux stew of redfish
leaves: the Creole courtbouillon belongs to courtbouillon
poaching as a method belongs to poaching

entries.title: Glace de viande and the glaces
covers: A glace is stock reduced until syrupy, setting firm when cold: glace de viande from brown stock, glace de volaille from chicken, glace de poisson from fish
The reduction: roughly 8 to 10 litres of stock to 1 of glace, skimmed, strained and moved to smaller pans as it reduces
Uses: a spoonful to deepen a pan sauce, to make sauce Foyot from béarnaise, to turn suprême into sauce ivoire
Jus and jus lié: the roasting juices served as they are, or lightly thickened with arrowroot, the lighter brown sauces of the modern kitchen
Why a glace needs unsalted stock and a watchful eye: it scorches and concentrates salt
Keeping glace chilled in a block or in portions
leaves: the classical demi-glace from espagnole belongs to demi-glace
reducing to nappe belongs to finishing-a-sauce
the modern reduced demi-glace belongs to demi-glace

entries.title: Roux
covers: Flour cooked in fat in equal weights, the classical thickener of French sauces
The French colours: white (cooked only until the raw flour smell goes, for béchamel), blond (for velouté), brown (for espagnole)
Clarified butter for a French roux; oil or lard in Louisiana, where roux is taken far darker
The temperature rule: cool roux into hot liquid, or hot roux into cool liquid, whisked in, then simmered to cook out the flour
Thickening power falls as the colour deepens: a dark roux flavours more and thickens less
Proportion for a medium sauce: about 50 to 70 g each of butter and flour per litre (authors confirm against the recipe)
Roux and the guest: flour means wheat, so roux-bound sauces belong in the allergen conversation
leaves: the Louisiana colours from peanut butter to brick belong to roux-ladder
beurre manié and the other thickeners belong to thickeners-and-liaisons
the allergen conversation belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Beurre manié, slurries and liaisons
covers: Beurre manié: equal parts soft butter and flour kneaded together, whisked in at the end to tighten a sauce or braise
Slurries: cornflour (cornstarch) or arrowroot slaked in cold liquid; arrowroot stays clear and suits fruit, cornflour clouds and thins on long holding
The egg and cream liaison: yolks and cream tempered with hot liquid, then heated without boiling, as in a blanquette or an allemande
The liaison ratio: roughly three parts cream to one part yolk by volume, added off the boil and held below a simmer
Reduction as a thickener: water driven off until the sauce coats a spoon
The old binders: blood for a civet, vegetable purée, bread, and in Louisiana okra and filé
Choosing the thickener by flavour, clarity, holding time and what the guest can eat
leaves: okra and filé in gumbo belong to gumbo-thickeners
reduction to nappe belongs to finishing-a-sauce

entries.title: Clarifying: the consommé raft
covers: Consommé: a stock cleared by a raft of minced lean meat, egg whites, mirepoix and tomato
The method: cold stock and raft mixed, heated slowly while stirring, then left still as the raft rises and sets
The vent: a hole in the raft through which the stock bubbles gently and bastes it, never boiled
Ladling out and straining through damp muslin, then lifting every trace of fat
The marks of a great consommé: crystal clear, amber, deeply flavoured, with a light body from gelatine
Double consommé and the garnishes of the old menus: brunoise, royale, en tasse
Why the old London turtle soup was a clear consommé while the Creole one is thick and dark
leaves: the Creole turtle soup belongs to turtle-soup
the stocks belong to white-stock and brown-stock

entries.title: Seasoning and tasting
covers: Taste everything, every time: a clean spoon for each taste, never back into the pot
Salt early in a braise or soup, late in a reduction, because reduction concentrates salt
Acid as seasoning: a drop of lemon or vinegar lifts a rich butter sauce or a gumbo
Heat in Creole cooking: cayenne, black and white pepper and hot sauce as seasonings, not as a dare
Seasoning the plate as a whole: sauce, protein and garnish tasted together
Correcting a fault: too salty, flat, too sharp, too sweet or too hot, and what each calls for
Describing heat honestly to a guest, and when to ask the kitchen
leaves: the Creole spice and the hot sauces belong to louisiana-hot-sauces
holding sauce temperature belongs to holding-warm-emulsions

chapters.title: The Mother Sauces
chapters.intro: The five mother sauces of modern teaching, béchamel, velouté, espagnole, tomate and hollandaise, and the families of small sauces built on them, with the history kept straight: Carême's four, Escoffier's grandes sauces de base and the later five. At Brennan's nearly every plate is a lesson in this tree, from the hollandaise and marchand de vin on the Hussarde to the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand.

entries.title: The idea of the mother sauces
covers: A mother sauce is a base from which many small sauces are made by adding a flavour, a garnish or an enrichment
Carême's four in the early nineteenth century: espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel

Escoffier's grandes sauces de base in Le Guide culinaire (1903): espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate, with demi-glace and allemande beside them as working bases; hollandaise is listed among the smaller compound sauces, not among the base sauces (authors confirm against an edition)
"The five mother sauces", adding hollandaise, is later teaching from twentieth-century schools and textbooks; teach it as such and never put the five in Escoffier's mouth
The five by liquid and thickener: béchamel (milk, white roux), velouté (white stock, blond roux), espagnole (brown stock, brown roux), tomate (tomatoes), hollandaise (yolks and butter)
Mayonnaise as the cold emulsion that stands beside them
Why it matters on the floor: name the mother and most questions about a sauce answer themselves
leaves: each mother belongs to its own entry: bechamel, veloute, espagnole, sauce-tomate and hollandaise
Carême and Escoffier as people belong to careme and escoffier
the naming logic belongs to sauce-tree-logic
the Guide culinaire's own sauce chapter belongs to guide-culinaire-sauces

entries.title: Béchamel
covers: Milk thickened with a white roux, seasoned with salt, white pepper and nutmeg
The classical build: an onion piqué (studded with clove and bay) infused in the milk; some old versions add veal or stock
Thin, medium and thick by the weight of roux: medium coats a spoon, thick binds croquettes and soufflé bases
Cook it out: a gentle simmer of at least 15 to 20 minutes to lose the floury taste; strain; protect the surface from a skin
Faults: lumps (liquid added too fast or at the wrong temperature), scorching, a raw flour taste
The name tied to Louis de Béchameil, steward to Louis XIV, told as tradition rather than proof
At Brennan's: the creamed spinach may be bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel; confirm with the kitchen before saying which
leaves: Mornay, Soubise and the family belong to bechamel-family
the Sardou plate belongs to eggs-sardou

entries.title: Velouté
covers: White stock (veal, chicken or fish) thickened with a blond roux; the name means velvety
The build: blond roux, hot stock whisked in, simmered 30 minutes or more and skimmed off centre (dépouiller) to a clean, glossy sauce
Three veloutés by stock: veal, chicken (volaille) and fish (poisson), each the root of its own daughters
Rarely served plain: a working base, finished with cream, yolks, wine or butter
Faults: a greasy surface from poor skimming, a grey cast from a roux taken too far, a thin body from weak stock
Velouté soups: the same idea thickened and finished with a liaison
leaves: suprême, allemande and the daughters belong to veloute-family
the stocks belong to white-stock and fumet

entries.title: Espagnole
covers: Brown stock thickened with brown roux, with a browned mirepoix, tomato and often bacon or ham, simmered for hours and skimmed
The classical build: mirepoix browned, roux added, brown stock in stages, tomato, bouquet garni, a long simmer, steady skimming
Rarely served alone: it is the parent of demi-glace and so of the whole brown family
The name means Spanish, and the reason is disputed; tell any story as tradition
Faults: bitter from burnt roux or bones, gluey from too much roux, greasy from poor skimming
Why many modern kitchens skip espagnole and reduce brown stock instead, and what is lost and gained
leaves: the brown daughters belong to brown-sauce-family, bordelaise, marchand-de-vin and fortified-wine-sauces

entries.title: Sauce tomate
covers: The classical French tomato sauce: tomatoes cooked with salt pork or bacon, mirepoix, garlic and white stock, then passed
Escoffier thickened it lightly with roux; later versions rely on reduction alone
How it differs from an Italian sugo: stock, pork and mirepoix, cooked longer and sieved smooth
Daughters by addition: provençale (garlic, olive oil, herbs), portugaise (onion, garlic, parsley) and, in New Orleans, the Creole sauce
Choosing tomatoes: ripe Creole tomatoes in season, good tinned plum tomatoes the rest of the year
Faults: raw acidity, a scorched base, a sauce too thin to coat
leaves: the Creole sauce belongs to creole-sauce
the Creole tomato belongs to creole-tomato
the tomato in Choron belongs to choron-and-foyot

entries.title: Hollandaise
covers: A warm emulsion of egg yolks and butter, sharpened with lemon or a vinegar reduction
The ratio: about one yolk to 60 to 85 g of butter, a little water or reduction, lemon, salt and cayenne
Whisk the yolks with a little liquid over gentle heat to a thick ribbon, about 60 to 65°C, then add warm clarified or melted butter in a thin stream
Clarified butter makes a firmer sauce; whole melted butter a lighter, looser one
The cues: thick enough to coat and hold a line, glossy, pale yellow, warm and never hot
Faults: scrambled from too much heat; split from butter added too fast, or a sauce too cool or too thick
The name means Dutch sauce; no clear link to Holland has been found
At Brennan's: the rich, lemony half of the two sauces on Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen
leaves: mousseline, maltaise and the family belong to warm-emulsion-family
holding through service belongs to holding-warm-emulsions
rescuing a split sauce belongs to breaking-and-rescuing

entries.title: Béarnaise
covers: Hollandaise's sister built on its own reduction: white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot, tarragon stalks, chervil and crushed pepper reduced almost dry
The reduction strained or left in, yolks whisked over it, butter mounted in, chopped tarragon and chervil to finish
Firmer and sharper than hollandaise: the classic sauce for grilled and roasted beef
Credited by tradition to the chef Collinet at the Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye around 1836, named for Béarn, home of Henri IV; tell it as tradition
Faults as for hollandaise, plus a reduction left too wet (a thin sauce) or too sharp
At Brennan's: printed as French béarnaise on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, and the base of the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand
leaves: Choron and Foyot belong to choron-and-foyot
Paloise and the rest belong to warm-emulsion-family
the hanger steak plate belongs to hanger-steak-bearnaise

entries.title: Marchand de vin
covers: The wine merchant's sauce: in France, shallots reduced in red wine with demi-glace, or a butter of the same flavours
The New Orleans version: onion and plenty of garlic, often ham and mushrooms, red wine and beef stock, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce
Antoine's made it famous in the city; Eggs Hussarde made it a breakfast sauce
Its place in the tree: a daughter of the brown family, cousin to bordelaise
How to say it at the table: a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, never a bare reduction
At Brennan's: the dark, winey sauce beneath the egg on Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen; whether tonight's carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef
leaves: the brown family in full belongs to brown-sauce-family
the Hussarde build belongs to eggs-hussarde

entries.title: Choron and Foyot
covers: Choron: béarnaise finished with tomato cooked down to a thick paste, coral coloured, tangy and herbal
Named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef at the Voisin in Paris, remembered for his menu during the Siege of Paris in 1870
Foyot: béarnaise with glace de viande whisked in, tawny and deeper
Named for the Restaurant Foyot in Paris; many texts call the same sauce Valois, others draw a line between them, so teach both names
Why the tomato must be reduced: wet tomato thins the sauce and can split it
At Brennan's: Choron on the Eggs Sardou, Foyot on the Roasted Chateaubriand; say sho-ROHN and fwah-YO
leaves: glace de viande belongs to glaces
the plates belong to eggs-sardou and chateaubriand-foyot
Paloise and the rest of the family belong to warm-emulsion-family

entries.title: Demi-glace
covers: Classical demi-glace: equal parts espagnole and brown stock, reduced by half, skimmed and strained, often finished with Madeira or sherry
The working mother of the brown family: bordelaise, Robert, chasseur, madère and périgueux all start here
The modern shortcut: well-made brown stock reduced with no espagnole, lighter and clearer
The cues: glossy, coating a spoon (nappe), a clean meaty taste, no flour, no grease
Faults: gluey from too much roux, bitter from scorching, salty from salted stock
Bought bases and how a professional kitchen judges them
leaves: glace de viande belongs to glaces
the daughters belong to brown-sauce-family, bordelaise, marchand-de-vin and fortified-wine-sauces

entries.title: Bordelaise, French and New Orleans
covers: French bordelaise: red wine, shallot, thyme, bay and pepper reduced, demi-glace added, finished with poached diced beef marrow and parsley
Escoffier's red bordelaise and the older white wine version; the name for Bordeaux
New Orleans bordelaise: a different sauce of garlic, butter, often olive oil and parsley, spooned over fish, oysters or bread
Why the difference matters: a red wine sauce and a garlic butter call for different wines and promise different things to a guest
The pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish most likely belongs to the New Orleans family, with toasted pecans; confirm with the kitchen before saying so
The steakhouse classic: bordelaise with a porterhouse or entrecôte
leaves: the Pecan Gulf Fish plate belongs to pecan-gulf-fish
the brown family belongs to brown-sauce-family

entries.title: The béchamel family
covers: Mornay: béchamel with Gruyère and Parmesan, finished with butter and sometimes yolk, for gratins and glazing
Soubise: béchamel with a purée of soft-cooked onions; the older Soubise was onion and rice
Nantua: béchamel with cream and crayfish butter, garnished with crayfish tails, the sauce of quenelles de brochet
Crème: béchamel finished with cream and lemon; cardinal: with fish fumet, lobster butter and cayenne
The cheese and mustard sauces of the bistro and the American kitchen as later cousins
The sauce of Oysters Bienville as a New Orleans cousin: a cream sauce with shrimp, mushroom and sherry, gratinéed
The croque-monsieur and croque-madame as the everyday Mornay
leaves: the naming logic belongs to sauce-tree-logic

entries.title: The velouté family
covers: Suprême: chicken velouté reduced with cream and mushroom liquor, finished with butter
Allemande: veal velouté bound with yolks and lemon, which Escoffier also called parisienne

Poulette: allemande with mushroom liquor, lemon and parsley; aurore: velouté with reduced tomato; hongroise: onion and paprika with white wine; ivoire: suprême with glace de volaille, and Albuféra: ivoire with red pepper butter
The fish side: vin blanc (fish velouté or fumet with white wine, yolks and butter), Bercy (shallot and white wine), normande (fumet, mushroom and oyster liquor, cream and yolks)
Warm ravigote: velouté with a white wine and vinegar reduction, shallot butter and fines herbes
Sole Véronique's white wine sauce with grapes, the classical ancestor of the Redfish Véronique
Telling them apart by colour, gloss and taste
leaves: the Redfish Véronique plate belongs to redfish-veronique
the cold New Orleans ravigote belongs to ravigote

entries.title: The brown family
covers: Robert: onions cooked in butter, white wine and vinegar reduced, demi-glace, finished with mustard; charcutière is Robert with gherkins
Chasseur: mushrooms and shallot sautéed, white wine, tomato, demi-glace, tarragon and parsley
Diable: white wine and shallot reduced with demi-glace and cayenne; the French piquante: vinegar, shallot, gherkins and herbs
Lyonnaise: onions with a vinegar reduction; poivrade: a game mirepoix, vinegar and crushed pepper
Bigarade: duck jus or demi-glace with bitter orange juice and zest and a gastrique, the sauce of canard à l'orange
Grand veneur and the game sauces as the family at its richest
The pattern of the family: an aromatic, an acid reduction, the brown base, a finish
leaves: marchand de vin belongs to marchand-de-vin
madère and périgueux belong to fortified-wine-sauces
the Cajun sauce piquante belongs to sauce-piquante

entries.title: Madère, Périgueux and the wine-finished sauces
covers: Madère: demi-glace finished with Madeira, added late so its perfume survives
Périgueux: madère with truffle essence and chopped black truffle; périgourdine: truffle in slices or balls, sometimes with foie gras
Financière and the old garnish sauces built on madère
Fortified wine as a finish: Madeira, port and sherry added at the end and never boiled hard
Sherry in Creole cooking: aged sherry finishing a turtle soup, and the cruet at the table
Madeira as a glaze: the Madeira-glazed broccolini with the Creole Hanger Steak
Truffle words on a menu and what a guest can honestly expect
leaves: the turtle soup belongs to brennans-turtle-soup
the brown family belongs to brown-sauce-family

entries.title: The hollandaise and béarnaise families
covers: Mousseline (also called Chantilly): hollandaise with whipped cream folded in, for fish and asparagus
Maltaise: hollandaise with blood orange juice and zest, the classic with asparagus; Mikado: with mandarin juice and zest
Noisette: hollandaise made or finished with brown butter; moutarde: with Dijon mustard
Paloise: béarnaise with mint in place of tarragon, for lamb
Choron and Foyot as béarnaise daughters, and Valois as a second name for Foyot
Rare cousins, Arlésienne and Tyrolienne, named only to show how far the family runs
The rule of the family: an acid, yolks, butter, then one defining addition
leaves: Choron and Foyot in detail belong to choron-and-foyot

entries.title: Reading the sauce tree
covers: Every classical sauce is a mother plus a defining flavour, garnish or enrichment, and a finish
Names that promise a place: béarnaise (Béarn), bordelaise (Bordeaux), lyonnaise (Lyon's onions), normande (cream and cider country), Nantua (the crayfish of Nantua), Périgueux (Périgord truffles)
Names that honour people: Mornay, Soubise, Choron, Foyot, and why some attributions are legend
Reading backwards from a name to a build: given chasseur, name the mushrooms, tomato and tarragon
Where the tree ends: beurre blanc, pan sauces, the Creole sauces and the New Orleans bordelaise sit outside it
Why a server who knows the tree can describe any sauce on any menu
leaves: the old dish names in general belong to old-dish-names
the families belong to bechamel-family, veloute-family, brown-sauce-family and warm-emulsion-family

entries.title: Finishing a sauce
covers: Nappe: the sauce coats the back of a spoon and a finger drawn through leaves a clean line
Dépouiller: simmering off centre so fat and scum gather on one side to be skimmed
Passing through a chinois, or a tamis or étamine for the finest sauces
Tamponner: dotting the surface with butter so no skin forms while it waits
Holding in a bain-marie at the right temperature for each family: brown sauces hot, emulsions warm
The last adjustment: salt, acid, a piece of cold butter, a splash of wine or cream, and a final taste
leaves: mounting with butter belongs to monter-au-beurre
holding warm emulsions safely belongs to holding-warm-emulsions
reducing to a glace belongs to glaces

entries.title: The sauces in Le Guide culinaire
covers: How Escoffier ordered his sauce chapter: the grandes sauces de base, then the small compound brown sauces, the small compound white sauces, the English sauces, the cold sauces and the compound butters (authors confirm against an edition)
Which he called base sauces: espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate, with demi-glace, jus lié and allemande among them, after the stocks, glaces and roux that come first in the book
Where hollandaise and béarnaise sit: among the smaller compound sauces, not as base sauces
His simplification of Carême: lighter sauces, fewer garnishes, the brigade's speed in mind
Reading the old text: the editions from 1903 onward and the English translations, and why lists differ between editions
Using the Guide well: as a record of a repertoire, not a recipe to copy line by line
leaves: the idea of the mothers belongs to the-mother-sauces

chapters.title: Butter Sauces and Emulsions
chapters.intro: The butter sauces and cold emulsions that sit outside the five mothers yet carry half the menu: beurre blanc, brown butter, meunière, compound butters, mayonnaise and its daughters, vinaigrette and mignonette. A Brennan's cook mounts beurre blanc for the Redfish Véronique, browns butter for the crab claws and the turtle soup's spinach, and knows how to save an emulsion that breaks in the rush.

entries.title: Beurre blanc
covers: White butter: a sharp reduction of white wine, white wine vinegar and shallot, mounted with cold diced butter over low heat
No yolks: the butter alone, added piece by piece and swirled, makes the emulsion
The temperature window: warm, roughly 55 to 60°C; hotter and the butter oils out, cooler and it sets
A spoonful of reduced cream steadies it, a restaurant habit; purists leave it out
Credited by tradition to Clémence Lefeuvre near Nantes: the Loire's sauce for river fish
Variations: citrus, herb, red wine (beurre rouge), and the preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique
leaves: the Véronique plate belongs to redfish-veronique
rescuing a split sauce belongs to breaking-and-rescuing

entries.title: Beurre monté
covers: Butter emulsified into a little boiling water, whisked in piece by piece to a creamy, pourable liquid
Held at roughly 70 to 85°C it stays emulsified; hotter and it splits
Uses: poaching lobster and fish, keeping proteins moist at the pass, glazing vegetables, finishing sauces
How it differs from beurre blanc: no reduction and no acid, a neutral cooking medium
Holding it through service and when to make a fresh batch
leaves: mounting a sauce belongs to monter-au-beurre

entries.title: Beurre noisette and beurre noir
covers: Beurre noisette: butter cooked until its milk solids toast hazelnut brown and smell nutty, then stopped with lemon or by pouring it off
The cues: foaming, the foam subsiding, brown flecks, the nutty smell; seconds separate brown from burnt
Beurre noir: taken darker, classically with vinegar and capers, for skate and brains; truly black butter is burnt and bitter
Grenobloise: brown butter with capers, lemon segments and croûtons
Brown butter vinaigrette: brown butter whisked with acid and served warm
At Brennan's: the warm brown butter vinaigrette on the Louisiana Crab Claws, the brown butter spinach on the Turtle Soup and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle

components: Brown butter spinach and grated egg

entries.title: À la meunière
covers: The miller's wife's way: fish seasoned, dredged in flour, shaken, sautéed in clarified butter until golden
The sauce: fresh butter browned in the pan to noisette, lemon juice and chopped parsley, poured foaming over the fish
Fish that suit it: sole, trout, flounder, speckled trout, drum; thin, white, delicate fillets
The New Orleans meunière: a richer brown butter sauce, in some kitchens with stock, Worcestershire or a little roux; each house guards its own
Cues: dry fish, hot fat, the flour cooked golden, the butter browned only once the fish is out
Faults: a soggy coat from wet fish or a cold pan, burnt butter, too much flour

entries.title: Amandine
covers: Fish à la meunière finished with flaked almonds toasted golden in the brown butter
The almonds toasted evenly, lemon and parsley added at the last moment
Trout amandine as the New Orleans classic, and the American spelling almondine
Pecans as the Louisiana swap: the same logic with pecans in the butter
Tree nuts in the pan: a separate pan and a word with the kitchen for an allergic guest
leaves: the allergen conversation belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Clarified butter
covers: Butter melted gently so the water evaporates and the milk solids sink or are skimmed, leaving pure butterfat
Yield: about 75 to 80 per cent of the whole butter
Why cooks use it: a higher smoke point for sautéing and meunière, a firmer hollandaise, no water to spit
Ghee: the clarified butter of South Asian kitchens, cooked on until the solids brown and the fat tastes nutty
Keeping it warm and clean on the station

entries.title: Compound butters
covers: Beurres composés: softened butter worked with a flavouring, rolled in paper, chilled and sliced
Maître d'hôtel: parsley, lemon, salt and pepper, the classic on grilled steak and fish
Bercy (shallot, white wine and marrow), Colbert (maître d'hôtel with meat glaze and tarragon), escargot butter (garlic, shallot and parsley)
Café de Paris butter and the house butters of famous restaurants
Shellfish butter (beurre de crustacés) for Nantua and cardinal
At Brennan's: foie gras butter on the Duck Confit Waffle and house-made miso butter on the Crab and Corn Omelette
leaves: the waffle and the omelette belong to breakfast-at-brennans

entries.title: Mayonnaise
covers: The cold emulsion: egg yolk, mustard, acid and oil whisked into a thick, stable sauce
Ratio: one yolk comfortably holds roughly 150 to 250 ml of oil, added drop by drop at first, then in a thin stream
Everything at room temperature; a neutral oil, or part olive oil for flavour
Its place beside the mothers: the base of rémoulade, tartare, verte, andalouse and the New Orleans rémoulades
Faults: splitting from oil added too fast or a cold bowl; the rescue with a fresh yolk or a spoonful of water
Raw yolk and safety: pasteurised yolks in restaurant mayonnaise
leaves: aïoli and the French rémoulade belong to aioli-and-french-remoulade
the Creole rémoulade belongs to creole-remoulade

entries.title: Aïoli and the French rémoulade
covers: Aïoli: garlic pounded to a paste with salt and olive oil worked in, often with yolk; the Provençal grand aïoli
Rouille: aïoli's red cousin with chilli, saffron and bread, for bouillabaisse
French rémoulade: mayonnaise with mustard, chopped gherkins, capers, herbs and anchovy; céleri rémoulade
Tartare and gribiche: tartare with chives, classically on hard yolks; gribiche from hard-boiled yolks with capers and gherkins
How the French rémoulade differs from the New Orleans one: white and herby against pink, hot and mustardy
At Brennan's: the chive rémoulade on the Crawfish Meat Pies; which style it is, the kitchen says
leaves: the Creole rémoulade belongs to creole-remoulade

entries.title: Vinaigrette
covers: Oil and vinegar in a temporary emulsion, classically three parts oil to one of vinegar
Mustard, shallot and salt dissolved in the acid first, then the oil whisked in
Choosing the acid: red or white wine, sherry, cane or Champagne vinegar, lemon
Warm vinaigrettes of bacon fat or brown butter, and why warm dressings coat better
Dressing at the last moment: leaves tossed to shine, never to pool
At Brennan's: the brown butter vinaigrette on the Louisiana Crab Claws

entries.title: Mignonette
covers: The raw oyster's sauce: finely minced shallot in red wine or Champagne vinegar with cracked black pepper
Mignonette is also the old kitchen name for coarsely cracked pepper, which gave the sauce its name
A spoonful, not a flood: it should lift the oyster's brine, never drown it
Variations with citrus, cucumber or chilli; the preserved Fresno chilli mignonette at Brennan's
Its place beside cocktail sauce and hot sauce at a New Orleans oyster bar
Say meen-yo-NET; min-yuh-NET is also accepted
leaves: raw oyster safety belongs to raw-and-cooked-oysters

entries.title: How emulsions hold, break and come back
covers: An emulsion is fat dispersed in water, or water in fat, held by an emulsifier: lecithin in yolk, milk proteins in butter, mustard
Why warm emulsions break: too hot (yolks scramble, butter oils out), too cool (the butter sets), too much fat too fast
Why cold emulsions break: oil too fast, too much oil for the yolk, a cold or greasy bowl
Rescues: a spoonful of warm water whisked in; a fresh yolk with the broken sauce added slowly; cold butter to cool an overheated beurre blanc
When to start again: a scrambled hollandaise does not come back
The broken sauce as a calm teaching moment on the line
leaves: holding through service belongs to holding-warm-emulsions

chapters.title: Methods
chapters.intro: The cooking methods the classical kitchen names and the Creole kitchen uses every day: sauté, pan-roast, braise, poach, eggs to order, boil and blanch, en papillote, confit, roast, grill, smoke, fry, deglaze, mount with butter and flambé. Each Brennan's plate rests on one or two of them, so a cook who can name the method can build the plate and a server can say why it tastes as it does.

entries.title: Sauté and the shallow fry
covers: Sauter means to jump: small pieces cooked fast in a little hot fat, tossed or turned
The pan hot before the fat, the fat hot before the food, the food dry and never crowded
Sautéing fish: dredged or not, presentation side down first, turned once
Shallow frying: more fat and a coating, for cutlets and soft-shell crab
Sweat, sauté and sear: soft and pale, golden, a deep crust
At Brennan's: the sautéed Gulf fish on the children's menu and the cooked-to-order fish of the Pecan Gulf Fish
leaves: the pan sauce belongs to deglaze-and-pan-sauce

entries.title: Pan-roast and poêlé
covers: Pan-roasting: sear on the stove, finish in a hot oven in the same pan, baste on its return
Poêler: the classical butter-roast in a covered pot on a bed of matignon, basted, then uncovered to colour
Why poêlé suits tender poultry and the finest cuts: gentle heat from butter and vegetables, and a sauce from the pot
Arroser: basting with foaming butter, thyme and garlic as the meat finishes
Poêlé told from a braise and a roast: a covered pot with butter and vegetables but little or no liquid
Pan-roasted dishes on a modern menu, and how to say pan-roasted to a guest
leaves: resting and carryover belong to roast-and-baste

entries.title: Braise and daube
covers: Braising: sear, add aromatics and liquid partway up, cover, cook low until the collagen turns to gelatine
Cuts that braise: short rib, chuck, shank, cheek; the gelatine is the reward
Daube: the Provençal red wine braise, marinated first, cooked in a daubière
Liquid and heat: a lazy simmer, or a low oven of about 150 to 160°C
Finishing the braise: skim, reduce the liquid, thicken or mount it into its own sauce
At Brennan's: the short rib débris on Eggs Owen, braised in red wine until it falls into its gravy; grillades as the Creole braise
leaves: red wine sauces belong to marchand-de-vin

entries.title: Poaching, shallow and deep
covers: Deep poaching: food submerged in liquid held at about 70 to 85°C, below the simmer
Shallow poaching: fish on buttered shallots, liquid halfway up, covered with paper, finished in the oven; the liquor becomes the sauce
The poached egg: fresh eggs, deep water at a bare shiver, a splash of vinegar if wanted, about 3 minutes for a set white and flowing yolk
Holding poached eggs in iced water and reheating them for service
Fish à la nage and the Véronique style as poached dishes
At Brennan's: the poached eggs of the Hussarde and the Sardou
leaves: the egg dishes belong to eggs-hussarde and eggs-sardou
eggs fried, scrambled, boiled and in an omelette belong to eggs-to-order

entries.title: Eggs to order and the omelette
covers: Fried eggs by name: sunny side up (unturned, the yolk runny), over easy, over medium and over hard (turned, the yolk runny, jammy or set), and basted under a lid or a spoon of hot butter
Scrambled eggs: soft and creamy over low heat in the French way, or firmer with larger curds; off the heat before they look done, because carryover finishes them
Soft-boiled and hard-boiled: eggs lowered into simmering water for a soft or a set yolk, then cooled in iced water to stop the cooking and the grey ring (authors confirm the times)
The French omelette: eggs beaten smooth, cooked in foaming butter over brisk heat, stirred and shaken to small curds, rolled while the centre is still soft (baveuse), pale and unbrowned
The folded, filled omelette of the American breakfast, and why a filling goes in warm so the eggs need not overcook
The egg pan: kept for eggs alone, the right size for the eggs, the butter foaming but never brown
At Brennan's: the Crab and Corn Omelette, the soft-boiled egg on Eggs Owen, the sunny-side-up egg on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, and Egg Any Style cooked exactly as the ticket reads
leaves: the words on the ticket belong to ticket-terms

entries.title: Boil, blanch and steam
covers: Boiling: a full rolling boil in plenty of well salted water for pasta and for green vegetables cooked à l'anglaise
Blanching (blanchir): a brief plunge in boiling water to set colour, loosen skins, tame bitterness or part-cook for service
Refreshing (rafraîchir): straight into iced water to stop the cooking and hold the green, then drained well
Monder: blanching tomatoes, peaches and almonds to slip their skins, the first step of a concassée
Steaming: food held over boiling water, gentle and moist, keeping its shape and flavour; the basket, the combi oven, the leaf or paper parcel
Why green vegetables turn olive with acid and long cooking, and so cook fast, uncovered, in a large pot
Blanching bones and meat for a white stock: brought up from cold, boiled briefly, drained and rinsed of scum
leaves: poaching and the simmer belong to poaching
the sealed parcel belongs to en-papillote
the white stock itself belongs to white-stock

entries.title: En papillote
covers: Food sealed in a parcel of paper, foil or leaf and baked, so it steams in its own juices
Building the parcel: a bed of aromatics, the fish, butter or oil, a splash of wine, the edges crimped tight
Timing by thickness; the parcel puffs when it is ready
Opening at the table: the burst of aroma is the point of the dish
Banana leaf and other wrappers, and what each adds
At Brennan's: the Gulf Fish en Papillote in banana leaf with tomato, Castelvetrano olives and Louisiana crab
leaves: the Gulf fish belong to gulf-fish

entries.title: Confit
covers: To preserve: meat salted, then cooked slowly submerged in its own fat until meltingly tender
Duck leg confit: cured overnight with salt, garlic and thyme, rinsed, cooked in duck fat at about 85 to 95°C for hours
Keeping it under fat, and crisping the skin before serving
Confit beyond duck: garlic, tomato, fish cooked gently in oil
At Brennan's: Rohan duck leg confit on the Duck Confit Waffle
leaves: the waffle plate belongs to breakfast-at-brennans
the duck breast belongs to roast-and-baste

entries.title: Roast and baste
covers: Roasting: dry heat in an oven, high to brown, lower to cook through
Seasoning ahead, bringing the meat up from the fridge, searing first or last
Basting with the fat and juices for colour and flavour
Carryover heat and resting: why a roast comes out early and rests before carving
Doneness by thermometer and touch, and how the kitchen and the ticket speak of it
At Brennan's: the Chateaubriand roasted whole for two, and the Rohan duck breast roasted with its skin rendered
leaves: the Chateaubriand plate belongs to chateaubriand-foyot

entries.title: Grill and salamander
covers: Grilling: heat from below over coals, gas or wood; the bars mark, the fat drips and smokes
The salamander, the overhead grill (broiler) of a professional kitchen: fierce heat from above for finishing, glazing and gratins
Zones on a grill: hot to mark, cooler to finish
The salamander at work: Oysters Rockefeller, a glazed sabayon, a Mornay gratin
Chargrilled oysters as a modern New Orleans classic
Why British English says grill for both, while an American kitchen names heat from above separately

entries.title: Smoking, hot and cold
covers: Smoke as flavour and as preserver: wood smoulders, and its compounds colour and season the surface of the food
Hot smoking cooks as it smokes: andouille, tasso, smoked sausage and hot-smoked fish
Cold smoking flavours without cooking, for salmon, cheese and some hams, and always follows a cure (authors confirm the temperatures)
The woods: hickory, pecan, oak and fruitwoods; resinous softwoods give a bitter, sooty smoke
Smoke at the pass: a smoking gun or a cloche over a liquid, a vegetable or a dressing, a seasoning rather than a preserving
The Cajun smokehouse and the boucherie, where the smoked meats of Acadiana come from
At Brennan's: the smoked tomato water of the Creole Tomato Tostada, the smoked oyster dressing of the Creole Caesar, the smoked potato pavé with the hanger steak and the Smoked Cauliflower
leaves: why New Orleans barbecue shrimp are never smoked belongs to barbecue-shrimp

components: Okra tostada and smoked tomato water

entries.title: Frying and the fry station
covers: Deep frying in clean oil at about 170 to 190°C: the oil drives off surface water fast and sets a crisp crust
The standard breading: flour, egg wash, crumbs; or the Louisiana cornmeal dredge
Small batches so the oil holds its heat; drained on a rack, salted at once
Oil care: filtering, skimming, changing; what its colour and smell tell you
Shared fryers and cross-contact: shellfish, fish and wheat in the same oil
At Brennan's: the popcorn shrimp, the crispy artichokes on the Sardou, the fried poussin, Brabant potatoes and French fries
leaves: the allergen conversation belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Deglaze and the pan sauce
covers: Fond: the browned juices left in the pan after searing, the base of the sauce
Pour off excess fat, sweat shallot, deglaze with wine, stock or spirit, scraping up the fond
Reduce, add stock or cream, reduce again to nappe, mount with cold butter off the heat
Cream sauces may boil; butter-finished sauces must not
The mustard cream of poulet à la moutarde: shallot, white wine, cream, and mustard stirred in off the heat so it keeps its bite
At Brennan's: the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin à la Moutarde
leaves: flambé pan sauces belong to flambe
the last adjustments belong to finishing-a-sauce

entries.title: Monter au beurre
covers: To mount with butter: cold butter swirled or whisked into a hot sauce, off the boil, at the last moment
What it gives: gloss, body, a rounder taste and a light emulsion
The rule: cold butter, a hot but not boiling sauce, butter in pieces, served soon; reboiling breaks it
Mounting a red wine jus, a pan sauce or a marchand de vin before it goes out
Mounting a sauce against making a beurre blanc or a beurre monté
leaves: the pan sauce belongs to deglaze-and-pan-sauce

entries.title: Flambé
covers: Flamber: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so its vapour burns in a burst of flame
What it does: burns off some (never all) of the alcohol, caramelises the surface, adds aroma and theatre
Strength matters: spirits around 40 per cent alcohol light well; weaker ones may not, stronger ones flare
Kitchen technique: pan off the flame, spirit from a measure, back to the heat and tilted to ignite, a lid ready
The classics: steak au poivre and steak Diane, crêpes Suzette, cherries jubilee, Bananas Foster
The flambé pan sauce of brandy and green peppercorn
leaves: the Foster at the table belongs to bananas-foster-at-the-table
safety at the table belongs to flambe-safety
