chapters.title: Creole and Cajun
chapters.intro: Louisiana's two great cooking traditions, Creole from the city and Cajun from the country, and the dishes they share and argue over: the trinity, the roux ladder, gumbo, étouffée, jambalaya, courtbouillon, sauce piquante, the Creole sauces and blackening. Brennan's is a Creole house that borrows Cajun pantry staples, so its gumbo, turtle soup, Creole sauce and rice dressing all start here.

entries.title: Creole and Cajun
covers: Creole: the cooking of New Orleans households and restaurants, French in technique, shaped by Spanish, West African, Caribbean, German and Italian cooks; butter, cream and tomato
Cajun: the country cooking of the Acadians, expelled from Acadia from 1755 and settled on Louisiana's bayous and prairies from the 1760s; smoked meats, dark roux, rice and game
What they share: the trinity, roux, gumbo and rice, and the line that blurs in every kitchen
Who "Creole" means: a layered and sometimes contested word, used by people of many backgrounds born in colonial Louisiana; say it with care
How Paul Prudhomme's fame in the 1980s blurred the two for the rest of the country
The one-line answer at the table: Creole is the city, Cajun the country, and the Brennan's menu is the city with country seasoning
leaves: the roots of Creole cooking belong to creole-roots

entries.title: The holy trinity and the mirepoix
covers: The trinity: onion, celery and green pepper (the bell pepper), diced and softened together at the start of a Creole or Cajun dish
Mirepoix: onion, carrot and celery, classically two parts onion to one each of carrot and celery by weight
Why green pepper took the carrot's place in Louisiana, and the ratio arguments: equal parts, or heavier on onion
Garlic as "the pope", and green onion (spring onion) and parsley as the finishing herbs
Cooking the trinity: into hot roux to stop its browning, or sweated in fat for a Creole sauce
The name most likely popularised by Paul Prudhomme; the white mirepoix and the matignon as French cousins
At Brennan's: in the gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce on the shrimp and grits, and the rice dressing
leaves: the roux ladder belongs to roux-ladder
cutting the trinity belongs to knife-cuts

entries.title: The roux ladder
covers: The Louisiana colours: white, blond, peanut butter, milk chocolate (medium brown), dark chocolate (brick)
Rough times over a medium flame in a heavy pot: blond 5 to 10 minutes, peanut butter 15 to 20, milk chocolate 25 to 35, dark chocolate 40 or more; the oven roux as a slower, safer path
Oil or lard for a dark roux (butter burns), equal weights of fat and flour, a flat wooden spoon or whisk, and never stop stirring
Smell and colour as the cues: black flecks or a burnt smell mean start again
Stopping the roux: the trinity goes in to cool it and halt the browning; hot roux burns badly, so no splashing and no tasting

Darker roux, more flavour, less thickening, and why: long heat breaks the flour's starch into shorter chains (dextrins) that brown and taste toasty but can no longer swell and bind, so a gumbo needs more of a dark roux than a sauce needs of a blond
Which dish wants which rung, and why the kitchen decides how dark each house roux goes
leaves: the French white and blond roux belong to roux
the allergen side of flour belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Gumbo
covers: A Louisiana soup-stew served over rice, thickened with roux, okra, filé or a mix of them
The name: most likely from a West African word for okra (ki-ngombo); a Choctaw word for filé (kombo) is the other theory
The families: seafood, chicken and andouille, duck and sausage, z'herbes
Creole gumbos often carry tomato and seafood; Cajun gumbos lean to dark roux, poultry and smoked sausage, rarely tomato
Rice in the bowl, never cooked in the pot; potato salad alongside in some Cajun homes
How a gumbo tells Louisiana's history: French roux, West African okra, Choctaw filé, Spanish and German hands
leaves: the Brennan's gumbo belongs to brennans-seafood-gumbo

entries.title: Roux, okra and filé
covers: Roux: the base of nearly every modern gumbo, made first, with the trinity cooked in it
Okra: sliced and cooked down until its mucilage (the rope) cooks out and thickens the pot; smothered first in fat to tame it
Filé: ground dried sassafras leaves, stirred in off the heat or at the table; boiled, it turns stringy
The old rule that okra and filé are not used together, and the cooks who break it
The seasons of the old households: okra in summer, filé in winter
Telling a guest how tonight's gumbo is thickened, and when to ask the kitchen
leaves: roux belongs to roux and roux-ladder
filé the ingredient belongs to file
okra the ingredient belongs to okra

entries.title: Seafood gumbo
covers: A Creole seafood gumbo: dark roux, the trinity, garlic, a stock of shrimp shells and crab bodies, often tomato, bay, thyme and cayenne
Andouille or smoked sausage for depth in many versions
The seafood goes in last: shrimp for a few minutes, crab claws and lump, oysters and their liquor until the edges curl
Okra in the Creole tradition; filé at the table for some
Holding and reheating without overcooking the seafood: the base held, the seafood added later in some kitchens
Serving: over rice, green onion and parsley over the top
leaves: the Brennan's gumbo belongs to brennans-seafood-gumbo
cooling gumbo safely belongs to cooling-stocks-and-sauces

components: Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat

entries.title: Gumbo z'herbes
covers: Green gumbo: many greens, collards, mustard, turnip tops, spinach, cabbage, cooked down and chopped or puréed
Lenten roots: once a meatless dish for Good Friday, now often rich with meat for Holy Thursday
The odd number of greens for luck, a custom tied to Leah Chase's Holy Thursday gumbo at Dooky Chase's
Its name from aux herbes, and its kin among West African and Caribbean green stews such as callaloo
Roux or no roux; smoked meats, sausage and ham in the modern versions
leaves: gumbo in general belongs to gumbo

entries.title: Étouffée
covers: Smothered: crawfish or shrimp in a thick, buttery sauce of blond to peanut butter roux, the trinity and stock, served over rice
Crawfish fat (the yellow hepatopancreas) as the flavour of a Cajun crawfish étouffée
Breaux Bridge and the Cajun claim; Creole versions with tomato
A butter roux, or the roux-less style thickened by butter and fat alone
Stock from the shells, cayenne to season, green onion and parsley to finish
How it differs from gumbo: thicker, a sauce rather than a soup, a lighter roux; and from a Cajun stew or fricassée: those take a darker roux and more gravy, while an étouffée is smothered thick
leaves: the roux ladder belongs to roux-ladder

entries.title: Jambalaya, red and brown
covers: Rice cooked in one pot with meat, seafood or both, the grains drinking the stock
Red Creole jambalaya with tomato, from the city; brown Cajun jambalaya with no tomato, its colour from well-browned meat and onions, from the country
Gonzales as the self-styled Jambalaya Capital, and the great outdoor pots
Ratio and method: long-grain rice to liquid about 1 to 1.5 or 2 by volume depending on the rice; lid on and no stirring once the rice is in
Kin to Spanish paella and West African jollof; the origin of the name is disputed
Faults: mushy rice from stirring or too much liquid, a scorched bottom
leaves: rice and rice dressing belong to louisiana-rice

entries.title: Creole courtbouillon
covers: Redfish courtbouillon: fish cooked in a thick tomato and roux gravy with the trinity, garlic, bay, lemon and wine, and allspice in some old recipes
Said coo-bee-YON in Louisiana: the French word, a different dish
Creole versions rich with tomato and roux; Cajun versions with catfish or redfish and less roux
In the old texts: courtbouillon in La Cuisine Créole and the Picayune's Creole Cook Book
Serving over rice, the fish whole or in steaks
leaves: the French court-bouillon belongs to court-bouillon-and-nage
the Gulf fish belong to gulf-fish
the old cookbooks belong to hearn-la-cuisine-creole and picayune-creole-cook-book

entries.title: Sauce piquante
covers: A Cajun stew: dark roux, the trinity, tomato and plenty of pepper, simmered long with game, turtle, alligator, chicken or shrimp
Piquante means sharp: the heat of cayenne and hot pepper, sometimes vinegar
How it differs from the Creole sauce: a darker roux, more heat, a stew rather than a sauce
And from the French sauce piquante: a demi-glace with vinegar and gherkins
The sauce piquante cook-offs of Cajun country, and rice as always
leaves: the Creole sauce belongs to creole-sauce
the French piquante belongs to brown-sauce-family

entries.title: Creole sauce
covers: The New Orleans tomato sauce: the trinity and garlic softened in fat, then tomatoes, stock, bay, thyme and cayenne, simmered thick
Sometimes started on a light roux; some cooks add a pinch of sugar against the acid
The backbone of shrimp Creole, Creole omelettes and many fish and egg dishes
How it differs from an Italian tomato sauce (trinity and pepper) and from a Cajun gravy (bright tomato)
At Brennan's: the Creole sauce with tasso on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, smoky as well as tangy
leaves: the shrimp and grits plate belongs to shrimp-and-grits

entries.title: Creole rémoulade
covers: The New Orleans rémoulade: Creole mustard, paprika, cayenne, horseradish, lemon, garlic, celery, green onion and parsley
Red style: an oil and mustard dressing with no mayonnaise, as in some old houses; pink style: built on mayonnaise
Shrimp rémoulade as its great dish, on shredded lettuce
How it differs from the French rémoulade: pinker, hotter and led by mustard
One of the five New Orleans sauces the Brennan's courtyard turtles are named for
At Brennan's: the chive rémoulade on the Crawfish Meat Pies; ask the kitchen which style it is
leaves: the French rémoulade belongs to aioli-and-french-remoulade
shrimp rémoulade at the old houses belongs to shrimp-remoulade-and-arnaud

entries.title: Ravigote, French and New Orleans
covers: Ravigoter means to revive: a French ravigote is sharp with herbs, shallot, capers and vinegar
Cold French ravigote: a vinaigrette with capers, shallot and fines herbes, for calf's head and cold meats
Warm French ravigote, a velouté daughter, named here only to tell it from the cold ones
New Orleans crabmeat ravigote: lump crab in a cold, mayonnaise-based dressing with capers, Creole mustard, green onion and herbs, sometimes baked hot
Another of the courtyard turtles' sauce names, and how to tell a guest which ravigote is on the plate
leaves: the warm ravigote as a velouté daughter belongs to veloute-family

entries.title: New Orleans barbecue shrimp
covers: Never barbecued: head-on shrimp cooked in a pan sauce of butter, black pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon
Born at Pascal's Manale, Uptown, by the family's account in 1954, from a regular's description of a dish in Chicago; tell it as their story
A pan emulsion, buttery and peppery, neither smoky nor tomato; it breaks if it boils or sits
Bread for the sauce and a bib for the shells: how the dish is eaten

At Brennan's: the style on the Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the dinner tasting; the house recipe is not published, so Worcestershire questions go to the kitchen
leaves: the emulsion science belongs to breaking-and-rescuing

entries.title: Blackening
covers: Paul Prudhomme's technique from K-Paul's around 1980: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend and laid in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking
The spices toast to a dark crust in seconds while the inside stays moist: blackened, not burnt
The blend: paprika, cayenne, black and white pepper, garlic and onion powder, thyme, oregano and salt
Smoke and ventilation: done outdoors or under a strong hood; why home kitchens fill with smoke
The blackened redfish craze, the pressure it put on Gulf redfish, and the fishing limits that followed
At Brennan's: the Blackened Tofu; the butter in the classic method is why the kitchen confirms before anyone calls a dish vegan
leaves: the vegan question belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Grillades and grits
covers: Grillades: thin pieces of veal or beef round, pounded, seasoned, browned and braised in a brown roux gravy with the trinity and tomato
A Creole brunch classic served over grits, with roots in the country boucherie
The gravy: medium brown roux, stock, tomato, thyme, bay, a splash of wine or vinegar
Braising until fork tender, and holding without drying
Grits: stone-ground or quick, cooked slowly with salt and butter; cheese grits as the variation
leaves: grits on the Brennan's menu belong to shrimp-and-grits

entries.title: Red beans and rice
covers: Monday's dish: red kidney beans cooked slowly with the trinity, garlic, bay and a ham bone or pickled pork, on washday while the pot minded itself
Creaminess from mashing some beans against the pot, not from cream
Andouille or smoked sausage alongside; rice beneath or beside
Soaking or not, and why old beans never soften
A city's signature: Louis Armstrong signed his letters "Red beans and ricely yours"

chapters.title: The Louisiana Larder
chapters.intro: The Louisiana ingredients a Brennan's cook handles and a server is asked about: the Gulf's shrimp, crab, oysters and fish, the Cajun smoked meats, filé, okra, rice, cane syrup, Creole mustard, hot sauces, chicory, pecans and the city's French bread. Knowing where each comes from, when it is best and what it does on the plate turns a menu description into an answer.

entries.title: Creole tomato
covers: A Louisiana-grown tomato rather than one variety: the name covers tomatoes from the rich soils of the lower Mississippi, especially St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes
Season: late spring into summer, celebrated each June at the French Market's Creole Tomato Festival
Why it is prized: ripened on the vine, sweet, sharp and juicy, eaten raw with salt or in sandwiches
Cooking with it: Creole sauce, courtbouillon, tomato salads; tinned tomatoes out of season
At Brennan's: the Creole Tomato Tostada, raw over an okra tostada with smoked tomato water and burrata
leaves: the Creole sauce belongs to creole-sauce

entries.title: Gulf shrimp
covers: The Gulf's main species: brown shrimp (spring and early summer), white shrimp (late summer and autumn) and pink
Graded by count per pound: U-15, 16/20, 21/25; the smaller the number, the larger the shrimp
Head-on for barbecue shrimp and stock; heads and shells as the base of shellfish stock
Wild Louisiana shrimp against imported farmed shrimp, and why the menu names the source
Cooking cues: grey to pink and opaque, curled into a C; a tight O means overcooked
At Brennan's: in the gumbo, on the shrimp and grits, as popcorn shrimp and as fried Gulf shrimp

entries.title: Crawfish
covers: Freshwater crustaceans, mostly red swamp crawfish, wild from the Atchafalaya Basin and farmed in rotation with rice
Season: roughly January to June, at its best in spring; frozen tail meat the rest of the year
The boil: live crawfish purged and boiled in a fiercely seasoned court-bouillon with corn and potatoes
Tail meat and the "fat" (the yellow hepatopancreas) that flavours étouffée and pies
Louisiana against imported tail meat, and why the label matters
At Brennan's: the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost
leaves: live shellfish handling belongs to shellfish-handling
the boil liquor belongs to court-bouillon-and-nage

entries.title: Blue crab and lump crabmeat
covers: The blue crab of the Gulf and Atlantic; Louisiana lands a large share of the country's catch
Grades of picked meat: jumbo lump (the two large muscles by the swimming legs), lump, backfin, special (white body flakes) and claw (darker, sweeter, firmer)
Crab claws: cocktail claws served cold, or warmed in butter
Soft-shell crab: a blue crab taken just after it moults, fried or sautéed whole
Picking over for shell and folding gently to keep the lumps whole
At Brennan's: the warm Louisiana Crab Claws, lump crab on the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Crab and Corn Omelette, crab in the papillote and the gumbo

components: Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat
Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat
Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat
Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat

entries.title: Gulf oysters
covers: The eastern oyster, grown on reefs and leases in Louisiana's brackish bays
Salinity and flavour: fresher water gives milder, plumper oysters; saltier water brinier ones
Off-bottom farmed oysters such as the Grand Isle Jewel, grown in floating cages for clean, even shells
The R-month rule as history and its modern meaning: summer oysters are softer and spawning, and warm water raises the risk of Vibrio
Raw on the half shell, chargrilled, fried, baked Rockefeller or Bienville, in gumbo and dressing
At Brennan's: Grand Isle Jewel Oysters raw, Louisiana Oysters in barbecue sauce, oysters in the gumbo and the smoked oyster dressing on the Creole Caesar
leaves: raw oyster safety belongs to raw-and-cooked-oysters

entries.title: Redfish, drum and the Gulf fish
covers: Redfish (red drum): copper red with a black spot near the tail, firm and mild; black drum its larger, coarser cousin
The other Gulf fish a menu names: speckled trout (spotted sea trout), flounder, pompano, sheepshead, red snapper, grouper, tripletail, cobia, amberjack
The redfish story: the blackened craze drove heavy fishing, commercial limits followed in the late 1980s and red drum became a game fish in Louisiana (authors confirm the dates)
The Gulf fish of the day: learned at lineup, never guessed
Round fish and flat fish, fillets skin on or off, and pin bones
At Brennan's: Redfish Véronique, the Pecan Gulf Fish, the Gulf Fish en Papillote and the children's sautéed Gulf fish
leaves: pompano en papillote belongs to pompano-en-papillote

entries.title: Andouille
covers: Cajun andouille: coarsely cut pork with garlic, pepper and spice, stuffed in a casing and heavily smoked
LaPlace as the self-styled Andouille Capital of the World, and the German Coast's sausage-making
French andouille and andouillette: chitterling sausages, a different thing; warn a guest who expects the French
In gumbo, jambalaya and red beans: browned first so its fat and smoke season the pot
At Brennan's: smoky andouille in the Seafood Gumbo
leaves: the German Coast belongs to creole-roots
smoking as a method belongs to smoking

entries.title: Tasso
covers: Cajun tasso: strips of pork shoulder cured, rubbed with cayenne and spices and hot-smoked; a seasoning meat more than a ham
Used in small dice to season: Creole sauce, beans, gumbo, cream sauces for pasta
Say TAH-so; TASS-oh is also heard, so follow the house habit
How it differs from country ham and from andouille
At Brennan's: tasso in the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits
leaves: the Creole sauce belongs to creole-sauce

entries.title: Boudin
covers: Cajun boudin blanc: pork, liver, rice, onion, green onion and pepper in a casing, poached or steamed, eaten hot and squeezed from the skin
Boudin rouge, made with pig's blood, now rare in commerce
Boudin balls: the filling rolled, breaded and fried
The French boudin blanc (white meat and milk) and boudin noir (blood) as distant cousins
The boudin trail of Acadiana and the roadside counters that sell it
leaves: the Acadian story belongs to creole-and-cajun

entries.title: Filé
covers: Ground dried leaves of the sassafras tree, a Choctaw ingredient taken up by Creole and Cajun cooks
Taste and smell: earthy and woody, a little like eucalyptus or root beer
Buying and keeping: pure filé against blends cut with thyme or other herbs, kept sealed and used fresh, as it loses its aroma fast
Say FEE-lay; gumbo filé as the name for a gumbo thickened with it
Safrole, found mostly in sassafras root and bark rather than the leaves: health questions go to the kitchen, never answered from the floor
leaves: filé in gumbo belongs to gumbo-thickeners
the Choctaw contribution belongs to creole-roots

entries.title: Okra
covers: A pod of the mallow family, carried from West Africa through the slave trade; the likely source of the word gumbo
Mucilage: the slipperiness that thickens gumbo; cooked down long in fat to tame it, or fried fast to avoid it
Choosing: small, firm, bright pods; large ones turn woody
Fried okra, okra and tomatoes, smothered okra, pickled okra
At Brennan's: the housemade okra tostada under the Creole Tomato Tostada and the fried okra chips on the shrimp and grits
leaves: okra in gumbo belongs to gumbo-thickeners
the West African roots belong to creole-roots

components: Okra tostada and smoked tomato water

entries.title: Louisiana rice
covers: Rice country: the prairie parishes of south-west Louisiana around Crowley, the self-styled Rice Capital of America
Long grain as the everyday rice; popcorn rice, an aromatic long grain that smells of popcorn as it cooks
Cooking rice to stay separate for gumbo and étouffée: rinsed, measured water, covered, rested
Rice dressing and dirty rice: rice cooked with minced meat, giblets or liver and the trinity
Crawfish farmed in rotation in the same rice fields
At Brennan's: popcorn rice in the Seafood Gumbo and the South Louisiana Rice Dressing
leaves: red beans and rice belong to red-beans-and-rice

entries.title: Cane syrup and Steen's
covers: Pure cane syrup: sugar cane juice boiled down to a dark, glossy syrup, gentler than molasses
Steen's of Abbeville, making syrup in open kettles since 1910
Cane syrup against molasses (a by-product of refining sugar) and against sorghum syrup
Uses: on biscuits and pain perdu, in pecan pie and glazes, in gastriques and barbecue sauces
Louisiana's sugar parishes and the cane harvest each autumn
At Brennan's: the cane syrup-glazed peaches with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast

entries.title: Creole mustard
covers: A coarse, spicy whole-grain mustard of brown mustard seeds steeped in vinegar, often with horseradish
Its German roots on the river parishes; Zatarain's as the best known brand
Uses: rémoulade, sandwiches, glazes, crab cakes, vinaigrettes
How it differs from Dijon (smooth, white wine) and from yellow mustard (turmeric, mild)
Adding mustard off the heat to keep its bite
leaves: the mustard cream sauce belongs to deglaze-and-pan-sauce

entries.title: Louisiana hot sauces
covers: Louisiana-style hot sauce: aged peppers, vinegar and salt
Tabasco: the McIlhenny family on Avery Island since 1868, tabasco peppers mashed with salt and aged in barrels
Crystal: Baumer Foods of New Orleans since 1923, milder and more vinegar-forward, the city's table bottle
Hot sauce as a seasoning at the table: on oysters, eggs, gumbo, red beans
Creole seasoning blends and how they differ from hot sauce
At Brennan's: the Crystal hot sauce gastrique on the Popcorn Shrimp and the housemade Creole spice
leaves: seasoning by taste belongs to seasoning-and-tasting
the blackening spice belongs to blackening

entries.title: Chicory coffee
covers: Roasted, ground chicory root blended with coffee: darker, more bitter, less caffeine to the cup
A French habit brought to New Orleans; the Civil War blockade story told as tradition
Café au lait with chicory at Café du Monde and the French Market
Chicory the root and chicory the salad leaf: one plant family, different crops
At Brennan's: the chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate of the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake

entries.title: Pecans
covers: The native hickory nut, wild and in orchards across the South, harvested in autumn
Toasting brings out the oil and flavour; burnt pecans turn bitter fast
In the Creole kitchen: pralines, pecan pie, pecan-crusted fish, pecan butter sauces
Say puh-KAHN or PEE-can: both are heard in the South
Tree nut allergy: pecans travel through many dishes and sauces
At Brennan's: the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish, pralines with the bread pudding, the Baked Apple crumble and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake
leaves: the pecan bordelaise belongs to bordelaise

entries.title: Leidenheimer and New Orleans French bread
covers: New Orleans French bread: a thin, shattering crust and a light, airy crumb, lighter than a Paris baguette
Leidenheimer Baking Company, founded in 1896 by George Leidenheimer, the bakery behind most po-boys
The po-boy loaf, dressed with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise
Stale French bread as the base of bread pudding and pain perdu
At Brennan's: the Leidenheimer crisps on the Creole Caesar

entries.title: Mirliton, satsuma and Creole cream cheese
covers: Mirliton: the chayote, pale green and pear shaped, stuffed with shrimp and crab or ham for the holidays in New Orleans homes
Satsuma: a seedless, easy-peeling mandarin grown in Plaquemines Parish, in season from autumn into winter
Creole cream cheese: a soft, tangy cultured farmer's cheese eaten with sugar and cream or fruit for breakfast, nearly lost and revived by small dairies
Why the three matter: the household larder of old New Orleans, rarely seen on restaurant menus
Using them in season and talking about them with a curious guest
leaves: the Creole roots belong to creole-roots

entries.title: Eggs and yolks
covers: The egg as the kitchen's binder, leavener, emulsifier and sauce base: the yolk's lecithin holds hollandaise, béarnaise, mayonnaise and the tartare dressing
Grades, sizes and freshness: a fresh egg's tight white and standing yolk, why the poaching egg must be fresh and why an older egg peels
Pasture-raised as Vital Farms prints it, 108 square feet (10 square metres) of pasture a hen, against the cage-free and free-range labels

The ways the menu cooks an egg: poached on the Hussarde and Sardou, soft-boiled on the Owen, sunny side up on the breakfast hanger, grated on the turtle soup, cured as the yolk bottarga on the tartare cannoli
Raw and lightly cooked egg at the table: the consumer advisory said before the answer, and whether the yolk is pasteurised as a question for the kitchen
At Brennan's: the Vital Farms yolk on the fall Steak Tartare with Rye and the egg in its dressing
leaves: egg safety and the pasteurised answer belong to eggs
poaching, frying and the omelette belong to eggs-to-order

components: Vital Farms egg yolk, on the tartare

entries.title: Butter
covers: What butter is: cream churned until the fat gathers, about 80 per cent fat with water and milk solids, which is why it browns, burns and splits
Sweet, salted and cultured butter, European-style at 82 per cent and above, and why the kitchen cooks with unsalted
Butter's four jobs on the menu: the fat a pan starts in, the body of a warm emulsion, the gloss of a sauce mounted at the end, and brown butter as a sauce in its own right
Keeping it: cold for lamination and beurre blanc, soft for creaming, clarified for the high heat of a sauté
Dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen; butter travels through more plates than a guest expects

At Brennan's: the brown butter on the Swordfish Grenobloise and the crab claws, the butter that finishes the frascarelli on the Chateau Espagnole, the beurre blanc on the Véronique and the pan the Bananas Foster starts in
leaves: beurre noisette and beurre noir belong to beurre-noisette-and-noir
monter au beurre belongs to monter-au-beurre
how a butter emulsion holds and breaks belongs to breaking-and-rescuing

components: Bananas, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon

entries.title: Cream and crème fraîche
covers: Cream by fat: single and whipping at 30 to 36 per cent, double and heavy at 36 to 48, and why fat decides what whips, what boils and what splits
Crème fraîche, say krem FRESH, cultured cream that holds its body in heat and lifts a sweet plate with tang; mascarpone, say mas-kar-POH-nay, the Italian cousin
Cream in a sauce: reduced on its own until it coats a spoon, or stirred in off the heat; acid and salt added last so it stays smooth
Whipping: cold cream, cold bowl, soft peaks for folding and firm for piping; over-beaten cream turns to butter
Dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen
At Brennan's: the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin, the Creamed Spinach, the whipped crème fraîche on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and the cream set with gelatine in the fall Chocolate Crémeux
leaves: cream as a liaison belongs to thickeners-and-liaisons
Creole cream cheese belongs to creole-heirlooms
ice cream and the Foster belong to bananas-foster

entries.title: Mushrooms
covers: The cultivated kinds a kitchen buys: white button, cremini and portobello as one species at three ages, shiitake, oyster and king oyster; the wild kinds by season
Cooking them: a hot pan, no crowding, salt late, so they brown instead of steaming; a mushroom is mostly water
Mushroom liquor, duxelles and the mushrooms in a brown sauce: the marchand de vin's red wine and mushroom base
Preserving: dried, pickled and the kitchen's preserved shiitake, say shee-TAH-kee
Mushroom Maggie's Farm of St Francisville as the name behind the side; tonight's varieties and whether they are cooked in butter or stock are lineup questions
At Brennan's: inside the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen, the preserved shiitake on the Blackened Tofu and the Maggie's Mushrooms side
leaves: the marchand de vin belongs to marchand-de-vin
the brown family belongs to brown-sauce-family

entries.title: Red wine in the kitchen
covers: Which wine to cook with: dry, sound and drinkable, never a corked or oxidised bottle; the fault cooks in and the fruit cooks off
What wine does in a pan: deglazes the fond, brings acid and tannin, and reduces to concentrate; the alcohol largely cooks away but never wholly, so tell a guest who avoids it
The red wine sauces of the house: marchand de vin, bordelaise and the braising liquid of a short rib daube
Reduction rules: the wine reduced before the stock goes in, by half or more, and tasted for rawness
Red wine against white, fortified and beer in the kitchen: where each belongs on this menu
At Brennan's: the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the red wine-braised short rib débris on the Eggs Owen
leaves: the marchand de vin belongs to marchand-de-vin
Madeira, sherry and the fortified sauces belong to fortified-wine-sauces

entries.title: Capers
covers: The unopened flower bud of a Mediterranean shrub, picked by hand and cured in salt or brine; the caperberry is the fruit on its stem, a different thing
Sizes by name: nonpareil the smallest and dearest, then surfines, capucines and the large capotes; salt-packed rinsed and soaked, brined drained
What they do: a sharp, floral, salty bite that cuts fat, in the tartare dressing, the Grenobloise, ravigote, rémoulade and piccata
Fried capers: patted dry and dropped in hot oil until they open and crisp, a burst of salt on a buttery plate
At Brennan's: the capers in the dressing of the fall Steak Tartare with Rye and the fried capers on the Swordfish Grenobloise
leaves: the fry station belongs to frying

entries.title: Preserved lemon
covers: Lemons packed in salt and their own juice for weeks until the rind turns soft, translucent and perfumed: a North African larder staple the kitchen makes itself
Using it: the rind rinsed and chopped, the pulp mostly discarded; it is salty, so the dish is seasoned after it goes in
Where it works: a beurre blanc, an aïoli, say eye-OH-lee, a braise of fennel, a dressing for roasted vegetables
Preserved lemon against fresh lemon, lemon confit and Meyer lemon: what each gives a plate
The time it takes: weeks in salt and months in the fridge, so the curing belongs to the kitchen and the batch is a lineup question

At Brennan's: the preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique, the Smoked Cauliflower with preserved lemon and harissa, say huh-REE-suh, and the preserved lemon aïoli on the fall Fish Bouillabaisse

entries.title: Beef tenderloin and the Chateaubriand
covers: The tenderloin: the muscle along the inside of the backbone that does almost no work, so it is the most tender cut and the mildest; the filet mignon, the Chateaubriand and the tartare are all cut from it
Its parts: the head, the centre cut (the Chateaubriand, say shah-toh-bree-AHN), the tail; the chain and the silverskin trimmed away
Cooking it: seared, roasted and rested, served pink because it has little fat to carry it further; Prime, Choice and Select as the USDA grades and Creekstone Farms as the house's Black Angus supplier
Served raw: the tartare, say tar-TAR, hand cut or chopped, and the consumer advisory given first
At Brennan's: the Roasted Chateaubriand for two with sauce Foyot, the 12 oz (340 g) Chateaubriand on the fall Chateau Espagnole, the Steak Tartare with Rye and the tasting menu's Petite Filet Mignon
leaves: the Chateaubriand with Foyot belongs to chateaubriand-foyot
the hanger steak belongs to hanger-steak-bearnaise
the cuts by name belong to cuts-by-name

components: Cooking a Chateaubriand: sear, roast, rest

entries.title: Lamb and the shank
covers: Lamb, hogget and mutton by age, and why American lamb is larger and milder than New Zealand's; spring lamb as a season that no longer rules the market
The cuts by use: rack and loin for fast heat, leg for roasting, shoulder and shank for the slow braise
The shank: the lower leg, full of sinew and collagen that melts to gelatine over hours in wine and aromatics, the daube of Provence
A jus from the braise: the juices strained and reduced to a glossy sauce, here scented with star anise, orange and cinnamon
Lamb's flavour and the guests who hesitate: how to describe it (sweet, grassy, richer than beef) and what to steer them to
At Brennan's: the fall Lamb Shank en Croûte, say ahn KROOT, a lamb shank daube under puff pastry with the spiced lamb jus
leaves: the daube and the braise belong to braise-and-daube
the jus and the glaces belong to glaces

entries.title: Swordfish
covers: A large ocean fish of warm and temperate seas, sold as thick steaks: firm, dense, meaty and mildly sweet, closer to a cutlet than to a fillet
Buying and keeping: the bloodline trimmed, the skin off, a steak cut thick so the middle stays moist; the US Atlantic fishery as a recovery story a guest may ask about
Cooking it: grilled or pan-seared hard and taken off just before the centre turns opaque, since it dries fast; rested like meat
Mercury and the pregnancy question: a large predatory fish, so the question goes to the kitchen and the service note, never answered from the floor
Grenobloise, say gruh-nob-LWAHZ: the meunière's cousin, brown butter with lemon segments, capers and croutons, from Grenoble
At Brennan's: the fall Swordfish Grenobloise on a leek fondue with brown butter, lemon, fried capers, Leidenheimer croutons and parsley
leaves: the Gulf fish belong to gulf-fish

entries.title: Tuna
covers: The tunas a kitchen names: yellowfin (ahi), bigeye, albacore and bluefin, by colour, fat and price; what sashimi-grade means and does not mean
Raw service: the loin, the cuts by fat (akami, chūtoro, ōtoro), kept at the cold edge and handled fast; freezing for parasites as the kitchen's answer
Crudo, say KROO-doh, the Italian word for raw: fish sliced and dressed with oil, acid and salt, against ceviche, which cures in citrus, and aguachile, which drowns it in a chilli and lime water
The consumer advisory, said first, and the species and cut as lineup questions
Sustainability and the guest who asks: the fishery, the gear and the label are the kitchen's to confirm
At Brennan's: the fall Tuna Crudo with carrot and ginger aguachile, salsa seca, burnt orange, coriander, pickled pearl onions and Maldon salt
leaves: the consumer advisory belongs to cooking-temperatures
the Gulf fish belong to gulf-fish
raw oyster service belongs to raw-and-cooked-oysters
seasoning with salt belongs to seasoning-and-tasting

entries.title: Rye and caraway
covers: Rye the grain: dense, earthy and faintly sour, with little of the protein that makes wheat bread rise, the bread of northern Europe and of the Jewish delis of New York and Montreal
Caraway the seed: the warm, anise-edged flavour most people take for the taste of rye bread; a cousin of cumin and fennel, and a note in Montreal steak seasoning
The deli echo on the fall plate: Montreal seasoning (black pepper, caraway, coriander, chilli flake and mustard seed) and a rye tuile stand in for the deli's pastrami on rye
A tuile, say TWEEL: a thin, crisp wafer named for the French roof tile, here made with rye for crunch against soft beef and yolk
Rye flour against wheat: why rye doughs are sticky and dense, and why a tuile is the easy way to put rye on a plate
At Brennan's: the Rye Tuile and Montreal Seasoning on the fall Steak Tartare with Rye
leaves: New Orleans French bread belongs to french-bread
the beef and the tartare belong to beef-tenderloin

entries.title: Fresh pasta and agnolotti
covers: Fresh egg pasta against dried durum: soft wheat and egg rolled thin and cooked in a minute or two, against semolina and water extruded and dried, firm and holding its shape
Agnolotti del plin, say ah-nyoh-LOT-tee del PLEEN: Piedmont's small pinched parcels, plin being the pinch; a thin sheet folded over a filling and pinched shut
Frascarelli, say fras-ka-REL-lee: rough pasta pieces of the Marche, flour and egg loosely combined, boiled and finished in butter
Cooking pasta: salted water at a rolling boil, pulled a minute early and finished in the pan, the starchy water binding the sauce; butter and cheese as the oldest sauce
Conchiglie, the shells of the Shells & Cheese, as the dried contrast; the children's buttered noodles finished the same way
At Brennan's: the fall Agnolotti del Plin with pork, braised collards, ricotta, Parmesan and lemon pangrattato, and the frascarelli under the Chateau Espagnole
leaves: boiling and blanching belong to boil-blanch-and-steam
finishing with butter belongs to monter-au-beurre
béchamel for a cheese sauce belongs to bechamel

entries.title: Dark chocolate
covers: From bean to bar: cocoa beans fermented, roasted and ground to chocolate liquor; cocoa butter, cocoa solids and sugar as the three parts a percentage describes

Dark, bittersweet, semisweet and milk by their share of liquor: bittersweet at 35 per cent and above by the US rule, usually 60 to 72 per cent; milk chocolate with milk solids added; white chocolate with no cocoa solids at all
Cocoa nibs: the roasted bean broken into bitter, crunchy pieces, chocolate before sugar, not chocolate chips
Chocolate in the pastry kitchen: melted gently, seized by a drop of water, set by its own cocoa butter in a crémeux, say kray-MUH, or a ganache; tempering for shine and snap
Dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen; the maker, origin and percentage of the house bar are lineup questions

At Brennan's: the fall Chocolate Crémeux with cocoa nib crumble, lemon olive oil and Maldon salt, the bittersweet chocolate of the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake and the Bavarian milk chocolate of The Snickers

chapters.title: The Old Houses
chapters.intro: The signature dishes of the other old New Orleans houses, Antoine's, Galatoire's, Arnaud's and Commander's Palace among them, which guests at Brennan's know and compare. Each dish is taught on its foundations, the sauce, the method and the story, so a cook and a server can speak of the city's grand tradition with accuracy and respect.

entries.title: Oysters Rockefeller
covers: Created at Antoine's in 1889 by Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, and named for John D. Rockefeller for its richness
Oysters on the half shell under a green sauce of puréed herbs and greens, butter and breadcrumbs, baked or glazed under the salamander
Antoine's recipe is secret and the house says it holds no spinach; many other kitchens use spinach with Herbsaint or Pernod
Rock salt to steady the shells, a hot salamander, the sauce bubbling at the edges
Telling a guest the story without claiming the secret
leaves: Antoine's as a house belongs to antoines
cooked oyster safety belongs to raw-and-cooked-oysters

entries.title: Oysters Bienville
covers: Baked oysters under a rich sauce of shrimp, mushrooms, green onion and garlic, bound with roux and cream or yolk, finished with sherry, crumbs and cheese
Named for Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, who founded New Orleans in 1718
Its origin disputed: credited to Arnaud's and also claimed for Antoine's; teach the dispute
Its place in the béchamel family as a New Orleans cousin
Building and baking: the sauce chilled firm, mounded on the oyster, browned in a hot oven
leaves: the béchamel family belongs to bechamel-family

entries.title: Shrimp rémoulade and Shrimp Arnaud
covers: Shrimp rémoulade: boiled Gulf shrimp, chilled and dressed in rémoulade on shredded lettuce, a fixture of the old houses
Shrimp Arnaud: Arnaud's own version in its red rémoulade, the house's signature starter
The houses' versions compared: red or pink, led by mustard or by mayonnaise

chapters.title: The Brennan's Menu
chapters.intro: The Brennan's menu read dish by dish on its French and Creole foundations, so a cook can build each plate and a server can explain it from its sauce and method. It covers Eggs Hussarde, Eggs Sardou, Eggs Owen, Turtle Soup, Seafood Gumbo, Redfish Véronique, Pecan Gulf Fish, Roasted Chateaubriand, both hanger steaks, New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, World Famous Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee, and through the sauce family, the breakfast tradition and the menu read by method it reaches Louisiana Oysters, Louisiana BBQ Lobster, Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, Louisiana Crab Claws, Creole Caesar, Crawfish Meat Pies, Popcorn Shrimp, Poussin à la Moutarde, Gulf Fish en Papillote, Blackened Tofu, Roasted Rohan Duck Breast, Duck Confit Waffle, Framboise French Toast, Crab & Corn Omelette, Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, Steak Tartare Cannoli, Creole Tomato Tostada, Blackberry Trifle, Creamed Spinach, Cheddar Grits, Brabant Potatoes, Egg Any Style, South Louisiana Rice Dressing, New Orleans Bread Pudding, The Snickers, Lemon Tart and Pineapple Tarte Tatin, and from the children's menus the Sautéed Gulf Fish, Vanilla French Toast, Eggs Any Style and the plates with Brabant Potatoes. Plates with no French or Creole foundation of their own, such as the Roost Burger and the Cheese Board, stay with the house study pack.

entries.title: The Brennan's sauce family
covers: Every sauce on the menu mapped to its foundation: hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot from the warm emulsions; marchand de vin from the brown family; beurre blanc from the butter sauces

The bistro and the bar: mustard cream on the Poussin, mignonette on the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, brown butter vinaigrette on the Crab Claws, Crystal gastrique on the Popcorn Shrimp, the smoked oyster dressing (an emulsion in the Caesar way) on the Creole Caesar

entries.title: Eggs Hussarde
covers: The house's signature egg dish: poached eggs on coffee-cured Canadian bacon over housemade English muffins, with marchand de vin beneath and hollandaise on top
New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict, with a red wine sauce as well as the hollandaise

Older than the restaurant: poached eggs à la Hussarde were printed in 1895 (credited to Adolphe Gallier of the Hotel Brunswick in New York) and Escoffier gave a version; Brennan's made it famous from about 1950, so never say it was invented here
The name: hussard, the light cavalryman
The classic build and why each sauce stays distinct; the house's own stacking is confirmed at the pass

entries.title: Eggs Owen
covers: Short rib débris braised in red wine and pulled, a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, with the Hussarde's two sauces
The name: guests guess it honours Owen Brennan, but the menu does not say so and the house has not published it, so the story is confirmed at lineup before it is told

Foundations: the red wine braise, hollandaise, marchand de vin

entries.title: The Brennan's Turtle Soup

chapters.title: Pastry and Desserts
chapters.intro: The custards, doughs, meringues and sugar work of the French pastry kitchen, and the New Orleans desserts built on them: Bananas Foster, bread pudding, pain perdu, beignets and pralines. At Brennan's the Snickers is a Bavarian cream, the Lemon Tart wears a toasted meringue and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin comes with an anglaise, so a server who knows the pastry foundations can describe every dessert with confidence.

entries.title: Crème anglaise
covers: The French pouring custard: milk or cream with sugar and vanilla, poured over yolks and stirred over gentle heat to nappe
Ratio: about 8 to 10 yolks and 150 to 200 g sugar per litre of milk or milk and cream (authors confirm against the recipe)
Temperature: to about 82 to 84°C and never boiled, or it curdles; strained at once into a cold bowl
The base of ice cream, of Bavarian cream and of île flottante
Faults: curdled from heat, thin from undercooking, a skin from cooling uncovered
At Brennan's: the sweetened condensed anglaise beside the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, with a caramelised milk note

entries.title: Crème pâtissière
covers: Pastry cream: milk, sugar, yolks and starch (flour or cornflour), boiled to cook out the starch
Unlike anglaise it must boil for a minute or two, so the starch thickens fully and the yolk enzyme that thins it is destroyed
Ratio: about 4 to 6 yolks, 100 to 125 g sugar and 40 to 50 g starch per 500 ml milk (authors confirm)
Cooling flat with cover on its surface; whisking smooth before use
Derivatives: crème diplomate (with whipped cream), crème mousseline (with butter), crème chiboust (with Italian meringue), frangipane (with almond cream)
Uses: éclairs and profiteroles, fruit tarts, mille-feuille, the soufflé base

entries.title: Sabayon
covers: Yolks, sugar and wine whisked over simmering water into a warm, airy foam; zabaglione is the Italian original with Marsala
Ratio: about one yolk, 25 g sugar and 30 to 50 ml wine a person (authors confirm)
The cue: the ribbon, thick and pale, the whisk leaving a trail, caught before the yolks scramble
Savoury sabayon: made with stock or Champagne and no sugar, spooned over fish or oysters and glazed under the salamander
The same foam as the first stage of a hollandaise
Champagne sabayon over berries, and the gratin of fruit
leaves: glazing under heat belongs to grill-and-salamander

entries.title: Pâte à choux
covers: Water or milk, butter, flour and eggs: the panade cooked on the stove, then the eggs beaten in to a dropping consistency
A classic batch: about 250 ml liquid, 100 g butter, 150 g flour and four or five eggs, added until the paste falls from the spoon in a V (authors confirm the house standard)
Steam is the leavening: a hot oven to puff, a cooler one to dry, the door kept shut early on
Shapes: profiteroles, éclairs, Paris-Brest, croquembouche, gougères with cheese
Beignets soufflés (fried choux) against New Orleans beignets (a yeast dough)
Faults: flat (too much egg or too cool an oven), collapsed (underbaked), hollow but soggy (not dried)
leaves: New Orleans beignets belong to beignets

entries.title: Meringues: French, Swiss and Italian
covers: French: raw whites whipped with sugar added gradually, the lightest and least stable, baked dry
Swiss: whites and sugar warmed over a bain-marie to about 60 to 70°C, then whipped, dense and glossy
Italian: hot syrup at about 118 to 121°C (244 to 250°F) poured into whipping whites, the most stable, and the one served unbaked on tarts and in buttercream
Peaks soft, firm and stiff; why a trace of fat or yolk ruins a meringue and a clean bowl matters
Uses: toasted meringue tops, baked Alaska, buttercream, île flottante, vacherin, pavlova, soufflés
At Brennan's: the toasted meringue on the Lemon Tart

the soufflé fold belongs to bread-pudding-souffle

entries.title: Caramel and the sugar stages
covers: The stages by temperature, roughly: thread 106 to 112°C, soft ball 112 to 116, firm ball 118 to 120, hard ball 121 to 130, soft crack 132 to 143, hard crack 149 to 154, caramel from about 160 (authors confirm)
Dry caramel (sugar alone) and wet caramel (sugar with water); a little acid or glucose against crystallising
Colour cues: pale straw, golden, amber, mahogany; past deep amber it turns bitter
Stopping and loosening: cream or butter added off the heat, standing clear of the steam, because sugar burns are severe
Caramel sauces, crème caramel, praline, nougatine
At Brennan's: the rum caramel of the Foster, the whiskey caramel on the bread pudding, the caramel custard in the Snickers, the caramelised pineapple of the Tarte Tatin

Why the caramel must be smooth before the fruit goes in, and the rum warm enough to light

entries.title: New Orleans bread pudding
covers: Stale French bread soaked in a custard of milk or cream, eggs, sugar, vanilla and spice, often with raisins, baked until set
The balance of bread to custard: the bread saturated but not swimming, and rested before baking
Whiskey sauce: butter, sugar, egg or cream and bourbon, poured warm
Why New Orleans bread works: its light crumb drinks the custard
Doneness: set at the centre, a knife comes out clean, a wobble only at the very middle
At Brennan's: New Orleans Bread Pudding with whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines
leaves: the bread pudding soufflé belongs to bread-pudding-souffle

entries.title: Pain perdu
covers: Lost bread: stale bread saved by soaking in egg, milk, sugar and spice and frying in butter

Soaking time by bread: dense brioche longer, light French bread briefly
Cooking over medium heat so the centre sets before the outside burns; thick slices finished in the oven
At Brennan's: the Framboise French Toast on housemade citrus brioche with raspberry coulis and mascarpone mousse, and the children's vanilla French toast

entries.title: Beignets
covers: New Orleans beignets: squares of a rich yeast dough fried until puffed and hollow, buried in icing sugar
Café du Monde in the French Market, open since 1862, and beignets with café au lait
Origins told many ways, French, Ursuline, Acadian; tell them as stories
The dough: enriched with milk, egg and butter, rested, rolled about 3 to 5 mm, cut and fried at about 175 to 180°C
Choux beignets and the Creole calas (rice fritters) as cousins

entries.title: Pralines
covers: New Orleans pralines: pecans in a fudge-like sweet of sugar, brown sugar, butter and cream or milk, cooked to the soft ball (about 112 to 116°C), beaten and spooned
French praline: almonds or hazelnuts in caramel, named for the cook of the Duc de Plessis-Praslin; New Orleans made it creamy and used pecans
The pralinières, the Creole women of colour who sold pralines in the streets
Cues: beat until the gloss dulls and it thickens, then spoon fast before it sets
Weather: humidity can keep pralines from setting

entries.title: Bavarian cream
covers: Bavarois: crème anglaise set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, chilled in a mould

Folding at the right moment: the custard cooled until it begins to set, then the cream folded in
Flavours: vanilla, chocolate, praline, fruit purées; charlotte russe and charlotte royale built from it
Codified by Carême; it sits between a mousse and a custard

chapters.title: Kitchen French
chapters.intro: The French of the brigade, the line and the dining room: titles, stations, calls, the pass, menu words, prep words, the names of cuts, ticket terms and the old dish names that promise a garnish. entries.title: The brigade de cuisine

entries.title: Calls on the line

Timing a table: every plate up at once, hot food hot, sauces fresh

chapters.title: History
chapters.intro: The people, books and houses that made French and Creole cooking: La Varenne, Carême and Escoffier in France; the many roots of Creole cooking; the first Creole cookbooks; Antoine's, Galatoire's, Arnaud's and Commander's Palace; and the Brennans, Paul Blangé, Paul Prudhomme and Leah Chase in New Orleans. A server who tells these stories accurately, with dates checked and legends named as legends, gives a guest the city's history along with its food.

entries.title: La Varenne
covers: François Pierre de La Varenne, cook to the Marquis d'Uxelles and author of Le Cuisinier françois (1651)
The break with medieval cooking: fewer heavy spices, the natural taste of food, butter and herbs
Early printed roux as a thickener, the bouquet garni, and duxelles, named for his patron
Stocks (bouillons) as the foundation of sauces, and reduction
Why historians call it the first great book of modern French cooking, and the caution owed to any claimed first

entries.title: Carême
covers: Marie-Antoine (Antonin) Carême, 1784 to 1833, abandoned as a child in Paris and trained in pastry
Cook to Talleyrand, the Prince Regent, Tsar Alexander I and the Rothschilds
Pièces montées: architectural centrepieces of sugar and pastry
His sauce system: four great sauces, espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel, from which the others descend
L'Art de la cuisine française au dix-neuvième siècle and the codifying of haute cuisine
The chef's toque and other attributions to treat as legend

entries.title: Escoffier

Le Guide culinaire (1903): the repertoire organised and Carême simplified
The brigade system: stations working at once, the aboyeur at the pass
His grandes sauces de base: espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate, with hollandaise among the smaller compound sauces
Dishes credited to him: peach Melba for Nellie Melba, Melba toast, cherries jubilee, and Sole Véronique by tradition
Why the Brennan's menus read as a lesson in his sauce tree

entries.title: The roots of Creole cooking
covers: French: technique, roux, sauces, bread and pastry; New Orleans founded in 1718
Spanish: rule from the 1760s to 1803, peppers, tomatoes and rice dishes cousin to paella
West African: okra, rice skills, deep frying and one-pot cooking; the enslaved cooks who made Creole food
Caribbean: refugees from Saint-Domingue, many thousands arriving by way of Cuba in 1809 and 1810, with their cooks and flavours
Native American: Choctaw filé, corn, beans and squash, bay leaf
German (the German Coast's sausage and mustard) and Italian (Sicilian immigrants, the muffuletta)

chapters.title: Sauce and Seafood Safety
chapters.intro: Kitchen safety for the dishes Brennan's serves: warm emulsions, eggs, raw and cooked oysters, cooling stocks, the danger zone, cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory, shellfish, flambé at the table and the allergen conversation. These entries teach kitchen practice and the words a server uses; they never give an allergen or health verdict, because the kitchen always confirms.

entries.title: Holding hollandaise and warm emulsions
covers: The tension: warm enough to stay emulsified, cool enough not to scramble or split, so it is held in a warm, never boiling, bain-marie

Where the holding temperature sits below 57°C (135°F), the sauce is in the danger zone: many kitchens then use a written time limit (often 4 hours under time as a public health control) and discard after it, never topping old sauce with new
Pasteurised yolks lower the risk; the kitchen's written procedure and the local health code decide
Labelling each batch with the time it was made, in a clean container every time
Beurre blanc and clarified butter held with the same care
Signs to discard: split, skinned, a sour smell, past its time
leaves: the danger zone in general belongs to danger-zone
rescuing a split sauce belongs to breaking-and-rescuing

entries.title: Eggs and safety
covers: Salmonella and eggs: why runny yolks and raw-egg sauces carry a risk, highest for the very young, the old, the pregnant and the immunocompromised
Pasteurised shell eggs and yolks for poached eggs, hollandaise and mayonnaise, where the kitchen chooses them
The consumer advisory: menus note that raw or undercooked eggs may increase risk
Eggs stored cold, cracked or dirty eggs discarded, hands washed after handling shells
What a server says: describe how the egg is cooked; the kitchen answers the safety question
leaves: holding warm sauces belongs to holding-warm-emulsions
the allergen conversation belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Raw and cooked oysters
covers: Vibrio vulnificus in warm Gulf water: rare but serious for people with liver disease, diabetes, weakened immunity or low stomach acid
Louisiana requires a raw oyster warning where raw oysters are served, alongside the menu's consumer advisory (authors confirm the current wording)
Shellstock tags kept with the oysters and filed for 90 days after the last one is served
Cooked oysters (Rockefeller, barbecue, gumbo) carry less risk when cooked through; post-harvest processed oysters for raw service
Oysters kept cold and alive; any that gape and will not close are discarded
What a server says: the warning, plainly; never promise that a raw oyster carries no risk
leaves: oysters as an ingredient belong to gulf-oysters

entries.title: Cooling stocks and sauces
covers: The two-stage rule of the FDA Food Code: from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours, then to 5°C (41°F) within 4 more
Tools: ice baths, ice wands, shallow pans, dividing big batches, stirring
Dense pots such as gumbo, roux sauces and beans cool slowly and need the most care
Never a full, hot stockpot in the walk-in: it warms everything around it
Reheating for hot holding: to 74°C (165°F) within 2 hours
Labelling and dating every container
leaves: the danger zone belongs to danger-zone
making the stocks belongs to white-stock and brown-stock

entries.title: The danger zone and hot holding
covers: The danger zone: 5 to 57°C (41 to 135°F), where bacteria multiply fastest
Hot holding at 57°C (135°F) or above; cold holding at 5°C (41°F) or below
Thermometers: calibrated, cleaned and used every time
Time as a public health control: the written exception some kitchens use, with discard times
Steam tables and bains-marie hold heat; they are not for reheating

entries.title: Cooking temperatures and the consumer advisory
covers: The Food Code's minimum internal temperatures: poultry 74°C (165°F), minced meat 68°C (155°F), fish and whole cuts of meat 63°C (145°F), each held for its stated time (authors confirm against the current FDA Food Code)
Probing the thickest part with a calibrated thermometer, and allowing for carryover
Whole-muscle beef served rare at the guest's request with its surface cooked, and why minced meat and stuffed dishes are treated differently
Raw and undercooked by design: steak tartare, rosy duck breast, runny yolks and raw oysters, each served under the menu's consumer advisory
The advisory and its reminder: the mark on the menu that ties a dish to the warning, and who it matters to most
What a server says: ask the doneness, point to the advisory, never promise an outcome; the kitchen answers the risk question
leaves: hot and cold holding belong to danger-zone

entries.title: Shellfish handling
covers: Live crawfish and crabs: kept cool and damp, never in still water; dead ones discarded before cooking
Shrimp and crabmeat kept on ice or below 5°C, used by date, thawed in the fridge or under cold running water
Cross-contamination: separate boards, gloves and utensils for raw shellfish
Cooked crab claws and lump meat handled as ready to eat
Shellfish as a major allergen: shells, stock and shared fryers
leaves: the allergen conversation belongs to allergen-conversation

entries.title: Flambé safety at the table
covers: Measure the spirit into a small vessel; never pour from the bottle near a flame
Pull the pan off the flame to add the spirit, then return it and tilt to ignite, away from the guest
Clear space: no drapes, decorations or low ceilings above the guéridon; sleeves and hair back
A lid or a damp cloth within reach, and knowing where the extinguisher is
In a bright room the flame can be almost invisible: treat the pan as lit until it has clearly died
The burner off before leaving the cart
leaves: the dish build belongs to bananas-foster-at-the-table

entries.title: Cross-contact and the allergen conversation
covers: The major food allergens in the United States: milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy and sesame
Cross-contact: shared fryers, boards, pans and garnishes carry an allergen even when the dish does not list it
Hidden carriers on a Creole menu: roux (wheat), butter in blackening and sauces (milk), pecans in sauces, shellfish stock, Worcestershire (anchovy)
The server's routine: listen, write it on the ticket, tell the kitchen in person, carry the plate separately
Never an allergen verdict from the floor: a server never promises a dish is free of anything; the kitchen confirms every time
Diet questions, vegan, gluten, gelatine, alcohol, handled the same way

careme.note: Carême grouped the French sauces under four great sauces: espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel. Allemande is now taught as a daughter of velouté. Escoffier's Guide culinaire made tomate a base sauce, and later textbooks raised hollandaise to give the five mothers of modern teaching.
